summary.text: The absolute Euler condition implies that the Carmichael exponent of the modulus divides \(2n=m-1\), which forces the composite modulus \(m\) to be squarefree and hence to factor as \(m=de\) with coprime odd factors \(d,e\ge3\). If \(b^n=-1\), the Chinese remainder theorem then gives a unit congruent to \(b\) modulo \(d\) and to \(1\) modulo \(e\), whose \(n\)-th power has residues \((-1,1)\) and is therefore neither \(1\) nor \(-1\), contradicting the absolute Euler condition.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
m=2n+1.
\]
By definition, the hypothesis that \(m\) is an absolute Euler pseudoprime means the following three things:

1. \(m>1\);
2. \(m\) is composite;
3. for every integer \(c\) relatively prime to \(m\),
   \[
   c^{(m-1)/2}\equiv 1\pmod m
   \quad\text{or}\quad
   c^{(m-1)/2}\equiv -1\pmod m.
   \]

Since \(m=2n+1\), we have
\[
\frac{m-1}{2}=n.
\]
Thus the third condition says that every unit modulo \(m\) has \(n\)-th power equal to either \(1\) or \(-1\).

We will prove the stronger assertion that there is no integer \(b\) at all for which
\[
b^n\equiv -1\pmod m.
\]
This immediately implies that none of the bases \(1,2,\ldots,2n\) counted by \(a(n)\) satisfies the required congruence, and hence that \(a(n)=0\).

First observe that \(n>0\). Indeed, \(m=2n+1>1\), so \(n\neq 0\).

We begin with a structural consequence of the absolute Euler condition.

### 1. The modulus \(m\) is squarefree

For an integer \(r>1\), let \(\lambda(r)\) denote the Carmichael exponent: equivalently, it is the exponent of the finite multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/r\mathbb Z)^\times\), namely the least common multiple of the orders of all units modulo \(r\). We use two standard elementary properties of this exponent.

First, if every unit modulo \(r\) has \(K\)-th power equal to \(1\), then
\[
\lambda(r)\mid K.
\]
This follows directly from the definition: the order of every unit divides \(K\), so their least common multiple divides \(K\).

Second, if \(r\mid s\), then
\[
\lambda(r)\mid\lambda(s).
\]
One way to see this is that every unit modulo \(r\) can be lifted to a unit modulo \(s\). Indeed, start with a representative coprime to \(r\). For each prime divisor of \(s\) which does not divide \(r\), impose in addition that the lift be congruent to \(1\) modulo the corresponding prime-power part of \(s\). The Chinese remainder theorem gives such a lift, and it is coprime to every prime divisor of \(s\). Therefore the order of each unit modulo \(r\) divides the exponent of the unit group modulo \(s\), giving the stated divisibility.

Now apply the absolute Euler condition to an arbitrary unit \(u\) modulo \(m\). We have
\[
u^n\equiv 1\pmod m
\quad\text{or}\quad
u^n\equiv -1\pmod m.
\]
Squaring in either case yields
\[
u^{2n}\equiv 1\pmod m.
\]
Since \(2n=m-1\), every unit modulo \(m\) is annihilated by the exponent \(m-1\). Consequently,
\[
\lambda(m)\mid 2n=m-1. \tag{1}
\]

Suppose, toward a contradiction, that \(m\) is not squarefree. Then there is a prime \(p\) such that
\[
p^2\mid m.
\]
By the divisor property of the Carmichael exponent,
\[
\lambda(p^2)\mid\lambda(m). \tag{2}
\]
Also,
\[
p\mid\lambda(p^2). \tag{3}
\]
For completeness, (3) follows by considering the unit \(1+p\) modulo \(p^2\). If \(L=\lambda(p^2)\), then \((1+p)^L\equiv1\pmod{p^2}\). The binomial theorem gives
\[
(1+p)^L
 =1+Lp+\sum_{j=2}^{L}\binom Lj p^j
 \equiv 1+Lp\pmod{p^2}.
\]
Hence \(p^2\mid Lp\), and therefore \(p\mid L=\lambda(p^2)\).

Combining (1), (2), and (3), we obtain
\[
p\mid m-1.
\]
But \(p^2\mid m\) also gives \(p\mid m\). Thus \(p\) divides the difference
\[
m-(m-1)=1,
\]
which is impossible for a prime. This contradiction proves that
\[
m\text{ is squarefree}. \tag{4}
\]

### 2. A hypothetical solution \(b^n\equiv-1\pmod m\) is a unit

Assume for contradiction that some integer \(b\) satisfies
\[
b^n\equiv-1\pmod m. \tag{5}
\]
Squaring gives
\[
b^{2n}\equiv1\pmod m. \tag{6}
\]
Because \(n>0\), (6) implies that \(b\) is invertible modulo \(m\), or equivalently,
\[
\gcd(b,m)=1. \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, if a prime \(q\) divided both \(b\) and \(m\), then it would divide \(b^{2n}\). But (6) would also imply that \(q\) divides \(b^{2n}-1\), forcing \(q\mid1\), an impossibility.

### 3. A coprime factorization of \(m\)

Since \(m\) is composite, it has a nontrivial factorization
\[
m=de
\]
with
\[
1<d<m,
\qquad
1<e<m.
\]
Because \(m\) is squarefree, the two factors are relatively prime:
\[
\gcd(d,e)=1. \tag{8}
\]
To justify this, if a prime divided both \(d\) and \(e\), then its square would divide \(de=m\), contradicting (4).

Moreover, \(m=2n+1\) is odd. Therefore every divisor of \(m\), in particular \(d\) and \(e\), is odd. Since both are greater than \(1\), this gives
\[
d\ge 3,
\qquad
e\ge3. \tag{9}
\]

Reducing (5) modulo \(d\), we have
\[
b^n\equiv-1\pmod d. \tag{10}
\]
Also, (7) and \(d\mid m\) imply \(\gcd(b,d)=1\).

### 4. Construction of a mixed-sign unit by the Chinese remainder theorem

Since \(d\) and \(e\) are coprime, the Chinese remainder theorem supplies a unique residue class \(x\pmod m\) satisfying
\[
x\equiv b\pmod d,
\qquad
x\equiv1\pmod e. \tag{11}
\]
This residue class is a unit modulo \(m\). In fact, its component modulo \(d\) is \(b\), which is a unit modulo \(d\), and its component modulo \(e\) is \(1\), which is a unit modulo \(e\). Under the Chinese remainder identification
\[
(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^\times
\cong
(\mathbb Z/d\mathbb Z)^\times\times(\mathbb Z/e\mathbb Z)^\times,
\]
the class of \(x\) corresponds to the pair \((b,1)\). Thus any integer representative of \(x\) is relatively prime to \(m\).

Taking \(n\)-th powers in (11) and using (10), we obtain
\[
x^n\equiv b^n\equiv-1\pmod d, \tag{12}
\]
while
\[
x^n\equiv1^n\equiv1\pmod e. \tag{13}
\]
Thus \(x^n\) has deliberately mixed signs in its two Chinese-remainder components: it is \(-1\) modulo \(d\) and \(+1\) modulo \(e\).

On the other hand, \(x\) is relatively prime to \(m\), so the defining absolute Euler property applies to it. Since \((m-1)/2=n\), it requires that
\[
x^n\equiv1\pmod m
\quad\text{or}\quad
x^n\equiv-1\pmod m. \tag{14}
\]
We now rule out both alternatives.

If \(x^n\equiv1\pmod m\), then reducing modulo \(d\) would give \(x^n\equiv1\pmod d\). Together with (12), this says
\[
-1\equiv1\pmod d.
\]
Hence \(d\mid2\), which is impossible because \(d\ge3\).

If instead \(x^n\equiv-1\pmod m\), then reducing modulo \(e\) would give \(x^n\equiv-1\pmod e\). Together with (13), this says
\[
1\equiv-1\pmod e.
\]
Hence \(e\mid2\), which is impossible because \(e\ge3\).

Thus neither alternative in (14) is possible. This contradiction shows that the original assumption (5) was false. Therefore no integer \(b\) satisfies
\[
b^n\equiv-1\pmod{2n+1}.
\]
In particular, the set of bases
\[
1\le b<2n+1
\]
with this property is empty. By the definition of the sequence, its cardinality is \(a(n)\). Hence
\[
\boxed{a(n)=0}.
\]
